trails.trailTip: The walk circles the entire fort on a paved surface with little shade, so bring sun protection and water even for this short loop; ferry and seaplane schedules limit island time, so plan the walk around your boat's departure.
trails.didYouKnow: Fort Jefferson is built from more than 16 million bricks, making it one of the largest masonry structures in the Americas.

trails.trailTip: Spring migration (roughly April-May) can bring a surprising variety of exhausted songbirds resting in the scrub here — give them space to recover rather than approaching for a closer look.
trails.didYouKnow: Garden Key's scrubby coastal vegetation provides a crucial rest stop for migratory songbirds crossing the Gulf of Mexico each spring and fall.

trails.trailTip: The wall surface is uneven brick and can be slick when wet with sea spray, so watch your footing, especially with kids.
trails.didYouKnow: The moat wall was designed to protect the fort's foundation from both cannon fire and storm surge.

trails.trailTip: The dock ruins are fragile masonry, so admire them without climbing on what remains of the structure.
trails.didYouKnow: The coaling dock once refueled steam-powered Navy ships making the long, remote crossing toward Cuba and Central America.

trails.bestSeason: Typically Oct-Jan (closed roughly Feb-Sep for nesting)
trails.trailTip: As of September 2026, per NPS.gov, the sandbar and Bush Key remain closed to protect nesting sooty terns and brown noddies, a closure that typically runs from roughly February through September — check nps.gov/drto for the current reopening status before planning to cross.
trails.didYouKnow: The sandbar linking Garden and Bush Keys shifts with storms and currents, and sometimes disappears entirely.

trails.trailTip: Loggerhead Key isn't served by the main ferry landing, so you'll need a private boat, kayak, or the ferry's snorkel excursion add-on to reach it.
trails.didYouKnow: Loggerhead Key's lighthouse, built in 1858, still helps ships navigate the reefs that gave the Tortugas their treacherous reputation.

trails.trailTip: This is the park's main swimming and snorkeling beach — bring reef-safe sunscreen and avoid standing on coral when entering the water.
trails.didYouKnow: The clear water here sits above one of the healthier coral reef systems remaining in the greater Florida Keys region.

trails.trailTip: There's no shade at the ramp, so this short walk is best combined with the longer perimeter loop rather than visited alone in the midday sun.
trails.didYouKnow: The ramp once served Pan American seaplanes ferrying passengers to the remote fort in the 1930s.

animals.whereToLook: Bush Key's dense nesting colony, viewable from Garden Key's shoreline and moat wall
animals.viewingTip: As of September 2026, per NPS.gov, Bush Key remains closed to protect nesting sooty terns and brown noddies (a closure that typically runs roughly February through September); view and photograph the colony with binoculars or a zoom lens from the Garden Key shoreline or moat wall instead of crossing onto the closed sandbar.
animals.didYouKnow: Bush Key hosts the only significant sooty tern breeding colony in the continental United States, with tens of thousands of birds nesting each season.

animals.whereToLook: Nesting beaches on Garden and Loggerhead Keys, and surrounding reefs while snorkeling
animals.viewingTip: Sea turtle nests are marked and protected on park beaches — never approach a nesting female or emerging hatchlings, avoid flashlights or flash photography near a nest at night, and observe any marked nest site from a distance.
animals.didYouKnow: Loggerheads can take 20-30 years to reach breeding age, and females return to nest on the same general stretch of coastline where they hatched.

animals.whereToLook: Soaring above the fort and nesting on Long Key, which is closed to public access
animals.viewingTip: Frigatebirds nest on Long Key, which stays closed to protect the colony — watch males inflate their striking red throat pouches from a boat or the fort walls with binoculars rather than attempting to land on or approach the key.
animals.didYouKnow: Long Key holds the only nesting colony of magnificent frigatebirds in the continental United States.

animals.whereToLook: Shaded pilings and wrecks around Fort Jefferson while snorkeling
animals.viewingTip: These massive, curious fish often approach snorkelers on their own — let them come to you and keep your hands to yourself rather than touching or chasing one, since goliath grouper are a protected species that can be harmed by repeated human contact.
animals.didYouKnow: Goliath grouper can grow to over 800 pounds and were once so overfished the species is still recovering under federal protection.

animals.whereToLook: Seagrass beds around the moat wall and surrounding reefs
animals.viewingTip: Snorkel quietly and watch turtles graze seagrass from several feet away — chasing, riding, or touching a sea turtle is illegal and stressful for the animal, so let it surface and dive on its own schedule.
animals.didYouKnow: Green sea turtles are the only sea turtle species that is primarily herbivorous as an adult, grazing seagrass meadows much like an underwater lawnmower.

animals.whereToLook: Diving for fish near the moat wall and docks
animals.viewingTip: Watch pelicans dive from the moat wall or dock with binoculars or a zoom lens, and never feed them table scraps or bait — handouts encourage risky begging behavior around boats and fishing lines.
animals.didYouKnow: Brown pelicans plunge-dive from as high as 60 feet, folding their wings at the last moment to spear fish underwater.

animals.whereToLook: Resting on the sandy bottom near pilings and the swim beach while snorkeling
animals.viewingTip: Nurse sharks often rest motionless on the bottom — admire them from a few feet away while snorkeling and never grab, ride, or poke one, since even a normally docile nurse shark can bite defensively if harassed.
animals.didYouKnow: Nurse sharks can pump water over their gills while stationary, letting them rest on the seafloor rather than needing to swim constantly.

animals.whereToLook: Nesting alongside sooty terns on Bush Key
animals.viewingTip: As of September 2026, per NPS.gov, brown noddies nest alongside sooty terns on Bush Key, which stays closed to visitors through the nesting season (typically February-September); view the colony with binoculars from Garden Key's shoreline rather than crossing the closed sandbar.
animals.didYouKnow: Brown noddies build their nests low in shrubs rather than on open ground, unlike most of the terns nesting nearby.
